Often, we initialize our weights and biases of our networks near 0.
And this acts like a bias toward finding solutions that have, again, low norm solutions-- low norm parameter vectors.
And then there's a lot of interesting work on the implicit biases of gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent.
And so one idea here is that stochastic gradient descent-- well, gradient descent with a fixed step size kind of descend down.
But let's say that I have a really, really sharp well in my objective function, in my energy landscape.
Well, gradient descent can't go into a really sharp well if I'm using fixed step sizes.
It'll just jump right over it.
That well will be too small.
So what gradient descent with a fixed step size will do is it will tend to find these, what are called, flat minima.
So kind of basins that are low loss, but are low loss over kind of a large region of the parameter space that I'm searching over.
And these flat minima can be argued to generalize better than these narrow minima.
The narrow minima might be more like just a weird solution that got lucky, but the flat minima is one that will generalize better.
So I'm not going to go into all the arguments for why that's the case, but you can see these papers if you're interested.
But the optimizer is a critical part of the recipe too, and it can affect the generalization properties.
But I think all of what I've said so far is not actually the most important.
I think the most important is the following two slides-- is the architectural symmetries.
And we saw these in ConvNets and graph nets, and we'll see these in transformers and other models too.
So our architectures are built to have certain invariances.
Like, if I'm pooling over channels with a max pooling operation, I'll be invariant.
And my filters are like edge detectors.
I'll be invariant to the orientation of that bird's beak.
I'll fire regardless of what the orientation of that bird's beak is.
So max pooling achieves this invariance over the dimension we're maxing over.
Equivariances-- so graph nets and ConvNets have these equivariances.
If I permute the labeling of the nodes, then I will permute the predictions.
Translation equivariance-- if I have a filter, and I slide it across the image, then if I shift the image by some amount, I'll shift my predictions by that same amount.

So these are symmetries that are kind of built into our architectures that cause them to exhibit out-of-sample generalization, because I know if I just shift my image, it will respond in the way it was trained to respond on the unshifted image.
That's what the symmetry gives you.
And then this kind of compositionality I was mentioning before-- that the ConvNet and a lot of architectures, they factor this input signal.
They maybe chop it up into little components.
They learn something about every little component, but then the conjunction of components is just given by something that's defined by the architecture.
It's not learned.
The conjunction of the outputs of these little patch-wise filters, patch-wise predictors is not learned.
It's just you stitch them all back together.
So I think this is where really the real power and the real explanation of why things like ChatGPT, why they actually do these feats of generalization.
It's not so much in my-- well, I don't know.
But I think it's a lot about it factorizes the world.
It carves the world at its joints.
It factors its world into parcels, which are words, and sentences, and paragraphs.
And then compositions of these things will be arrived at not from learning, but from just how the architecture is built.
And then a lot of neural networks have domain knowledge that's baked into them.
For example, Sarah gave the example of the NeRF model, which is a neural architecture, but it uses equations of perspective projection, and it uses equations of light transport.
And these are built into the process, and so it will generalize to new viewpoints because it's using structures.
It's not just fitting to data.
It's data plus structure, data plus constraints.
And this is a drug discovery, drug prediction problem, where they've baked in structure.
They know about how drugs are supposed to interact with each other.
And the conjunction of fitting to data under structural constraints is what can allow you to generalize.
So I want to end with one final point, which is, well, maybe we can actually go back, ultimately, to this theory answer.
The theory answer is that the shortest program that fits the data will be the one that generalizes.
I said it's intractable, but what if we say, we don't have to find the shortest?
Finding the shortest is intractable.
Maybe we don't have to optimize for the shortest program, but we can just say a short enough program that fits the data will generalize.
And so this is something that I've just kind come back to over the years.
This is a conversation I had with Ilya Sutskever, who's well-known as one of the founders of OpenAI.
And so he had this thing he said, which is deep-- this is not a direct quote.
This is just the rough memory.
"Deep nets generalize because they find small circuits that fit the data."
And so at the time, I didn't quite get it.
I was like, small circuits?
What are you talking about?
Deep nets are huge.
Don't we need all of these inductive biases, and regularizers, and simplicity biases?
Like, that seems critical to understanding deep learning.
And we need to bake those in.
We need to put those in our models.
And he said, "no, no, no, it's OK.
Deep nets are finite.
That's enough.
Finite is small.
Anything finite will look small if you have enough data."
And I think that was a deep insight and maybe led to some of the success that he's had.
So I'll end there.
Thank you.

You'll be able to design experiments to differentiate deep net generalization from memorization, illustrate out-of-distribution generalization, and explain how architectural biases contribute to generalization.

segments.subgoal: Outline the fundamental questions and scope of deep learning generalization theory

key_points.text: Deep neural networks generalize to some degree, but the underlying reasons for this generalization are not fully understood.
Classical theories of generalization do not adequately explain the observed performance of deep learning models.
The generalization properties of deep networks are considered one of the biggest open questions in AI research.
The lecture will cover the definition of generalization, the generalization capabilities of deep nets, and the failures of classical theories.

key_terms.definition: Generalization is the ability of a model to perform well on data that it has not encountered during the training process. This concept addresses whether a model's learned patterns apply successfully to new, unseen examples.

segments.subgoal: Distinguish between empirical risk, population risk, and the concept of generalization

key_points.text: Approximation focuses on minimizing the empirical risk, which measures the fit to the training data.
Population risk (test error) measures how well a model performs on new samples from the data generating process p.
Machine learning can be factored into three topics: approximation, optimization, and generalization.
Generalization is defined as the gap between the training error and the test error.

key_terms.definition: Empirical risk is the average loss incurred over all of the available training data points. This measure quantifies how well a model fits the specific data it was trained on.
Population risk is the expected error when making predictions on new samples drawn from the entire data generating process. This represents how well the model performs in the real world.

Empirical test risk is the measure of performance calculated over a finite sample, such as a designated test set. Population risk, conversely, is defined over the entire population of observations from the data generating process.
Generalization is the question of how well a model performs on new observations after being trained. It addresses the difference between the error on the training data and the error on the test data.

segments.subgoal: Analyze how data and model structure influence generalization error

key_points.text: Training data must represent the full variation of the real-world distribution for a model to generalize well.
A memorization model, such as a filing cabinet, achieves zero approximation error but typically has high generalization error.
Some functions can fit training data well by chance without having a true underlying model, leading to poor out-of-sample predictions.
The central question of the course is whether deep neural networks possess generalization capabilities.

key_terms.definition: Generalization is the ability of a model to perform well on new data, which requires the training set to represent all the interesting aspects of variation that the model will encounter in the world.

Generalization error measures how well a model performs on new, unseen data, representing the difference between the model's performance on the training set and its true performance in the real world.

Memorization is the process where a model simply stores and retrieves the exact answers from its training data. This behavior is characteristic of models like the filing cabinet, which do not learn underlying patterns.

segments.subgoal: Design and apply experiments to distinguish deep net generalization from pure memorization

key_points.text: Generalization refers to how a model performs on unseen data, while memorization refers to what the model predicts on the training data points.
A counting experiment can estimate the required size of a 'filing cabinet' (a pure memorization model) needed to achieve a certain prediction accuracy.
Applying this experiment to LLMs suggests that the required cabinet size (100 trillion) exceeds the known training data size, implying non-memorization.
Applying the experiment to text-to-image models suggests a required cabinet size of 12 trillion, also indicating non-memorization.

key_terms.definition: Generalization is the ability of a model to make predictions on data points that were not included in the original training set. This process involves determining what the model does when presented with unseen data.

Memorization is the process of determining what a model predicts specifically on the training data points. Generalization, in contrast, concerns how the model performs on data points where no training data was provided.
Filing cabinet is a simple model type that memorizes training data by predicting specific values only for the points it has seen. For all other points, the filing cabinet predicts zero.

Large Language Model (LLM) is a family of advanced deep nets, such as ChatGPT, that are capable of complex prediction tasks. These models are used to process sequences of words as input and generate predictions.

segments.subgoal: Illustrate out-of-distribution generalization using deep learning examples

key_points.text: Deep neural networks can be trained to map inputs, such as sketches, to corresponding outputs, such as photos of cats.,
Classical machine learning generalization assumes that data points are independently and identically sampled (IID) from the same population.,
The deep net project demonstrated generalization even when presented with hand-drawn cats, which were out-of-distribution (OOD) relative to the training data.,
This ability to generalize to OOD data suggests a form of 'creativity' or a mechanism in deep learning that is not fully understood.,

key_terms.definition: Generalization is the ability of a model to perform successfully on data it has never been trained on. This concept is demonstrated when a model works even when given inputs that are systematically different from its training set.
Out-of-distribution input refers to data that is systematically different from the data the model was trained on. These inputs are outside the scope of the training population.

segments.subgoal: Explain how architectural biases enable generalization in deep learning models

key_points.text: ConvNets process input by chopping it into patches and independently processing each patch (S309, S310).
Decomposing a problem into independent components results in compositionality (S311).
Architectural constraints and biases allow models to achieve certain feats of generalization (S316).
Graph nets can generalize to new permutations of inputs because they are permutation-invariant or equivariant (S317, S318).

key_terms.definition: Inductive bias refers to the architectural constraints and biases built into a model that allow it to perform certain feats of generalization. These biases enable the model to generalize beyond what is strictly predicted by naive statistical learning theory.

Compositionality is a property where a system can take a new composition of things and factor them into independent components, such as patches. This allows the system to know what to do because it only needs to imitate the training data on those individual components.

Permutation-invariant describes an architectural property where a model can generalize to new permutations of its inputs. This means the model does not need to have seen every possible permutation during training to perform correctly.

segments.subgoal: Explain the role of Occam's razor in generalization theory and its mathematical limitations

key_points.text: Occam's razor suggests that the simplest model that fits the data is most likely to generalize the best.
The principle requires that the model must fit the data; otherwise, the statement is absurd.
A rigorous version of Occam's razor states that the shortest program that generates the data will generalize best.
Finding the shortest program is computationally intractable because it requires searching over the space of all possible programs.

key_terms.definition: Occam's razor is a principle stating that among competing explanations that fit the data equally well, one should prefer the simplest model. This principle suggests that the simplest model that fits the data is most likely to generalize the best.

The shortest program is a concept from algorithmic information theory that serves as a rigorous version of Occam's razor. This program is the one that perfectly fits or generates the data and is predicted to generalize best.

segments.subgoal: Compare classical overfitting with the phenomenon of double descent in high-capacity models

key_points.text: Classical overfitting occurs when increasing model capacity allows the model to fit noise in the data rather than the true underlying function.
Double descent is the phenomenon where, after initial overfitting, increasing model capacity further can lead to better generalization error.
High-capacity models are hypothesized to contain two components: a simple, generalizing fit and a spiking component that memorizes noise.

key_terms.definition: Overfitting is the scenario where a model finds fits to the data that are based on properties that do not generalize, such as noise or the specific batch of samples used. Overfitting occurs when a model with too many degrees of freedom fits not only the true data but also the noise present in the training set.
Bias is defined as the training error. The bias is one component of the bias-variance trade-off, which relates the total test error to the training error and the variance.
Variance is defined as the difference between the test error and the training error.

Double descent is a phenomenon where the generalization error of a model starts to improve again after initially worsening as the number of parameters increases. This suggests that the classical picture of overfitting is inaccurate.
Model capacity is the complexity of a hypothesis space, which is classically measured by the number of parameters. Having too many parameters can lead to the model overfitting the training data.

segments.subgoal: Explain the double descent phenomenon and its relationship to model capacity and regularization

key_points.text: Unlike polynomial regression, which has a provable closed-form solution, neural network solutions depend on random factors like initialization and mini-batches.
The double descent phenomenon describes how test error initially increases (overfitting) but then decreases again as model capacity increases past the interpolation threshold.
When a model has high capacity, implicit regularizers select the smoothest solution from the set of functions that perfectly fit the training data.
The complexity of a solution may be more accurately measured by the norm of the parameter vector rather than simply counting the number of parameters.

key_terms.definition: Double descent phenomenon describes a pattern where, after increasing model capacity causes test error to rise (classical overfitting), the error eventually drops again, leading to improved generalization performance. This occurs after the interpolation threshold, where the model can perfectly memorize the training data.

Interpolation threshold is the point, as model capacity increases, at which the model can perfectly memorize all the training data. This threshold marks a critical point in the double descent phenomenon, where the model transitions from fitting the data to potentially generalizing better.

Inductive bias is a pressure that selects a specific solution from the set of all possible solutions that equally fit the training data. This bias often favors solutions that possess desirable properties, such as smoothness.

Overfitting is the condition where a model's training error continues to decrease, but its test error eventually begins to increase. This occurs when the model has too much capacity relative to the data.

Capacity is a measure of the complexity of a hypothesis space, which can be quantified by the number of parameters or the computational effort (flops). Higher capacity allows the model to represent more complex functions.

segments.subgoal: Compare classical generalization theories (VC theory) with the challenges posed by deep learning

key_points.text: The number of parameters is not a reliable measure of complexity because a small network can approximate a complex function using only a tiny fraction of its parameters.
VC theory posits that generalization is likely if the number of training data points is much larger than the number of distinct functions in the hypothesis space.
The VC dimension (d) is defined as the maximum number of unique dichotomies (binary classifications) a model can apply to the training data.
Neural networks can achieve any possible dichotomy over a dataset, which results in an exponentially loose generalization bound that fails to explain deep learning's success.

key_terms.definition: VC dimension is a measure of capacity that counts the number of unique dichotomies a function class can apply to the training data. A higher VC dimension means the model can classify the training data in more different ways.

Dichotomy is a binary labeling of all the training data points, assigning each point to either a positive or negative class. This labeling is represented as a vector of assignments to positive one or negative one.
Hypothesis space is the set of all candidate functions or neural architectures that the learning algorithm is searching over. The size of this space is a measure of the model's capacity.
Generalization error is the difference between the training error and the test error, or the training error and the population error.

VC theory is a framework that relates the size of the training data to the number of distinct functions in the hypothesis space. This theory provides a guarantee that population error matches training error if the data size is sufficiently large relative to the hypothesis space size.

segments.subgoal: Explain how simplicity bias in the parameter function map drives generalization

key_points.text: Generalization requires the presence of some kind of inductive bias (690).
The version space is defined as the set of all hypotheses within the hypothesis space that perfectly fit the training data (711).
The parameter function map is a many-to-one mapping, meaning multiple parameter vectors can define the same function (725).
Empirically, most random parameter settings in a neural network tend to map to simple functions (731, 744).

key_terms.definition: Inductive bias is the necessary assumption or rule that allows a model to generalize beyond the training data. It is the mechanism that rules out solutions that merely memorize the training points without making predictions about unseen samples.

The version space is the set of all hypotheses within the hypothesis space that perfectly fit the given training data. In neural networks, this is the set of all parameter settings that achieve zero training error.

The parameter function map is the relationship that connects the parameters (weights and biases) of a model to the actual mathematical function that the model defines. This map is many-to-one, meaning multiple parameter vectors can define the same function.

Simplicity bias is the empirical observation that when parameters are randomly sampled in a neural network, the resulting functions tend to be simple according to complexity measures like Lempel-Ziv complexity. This means that most random settings of weights and biases map to functions that are compressible, rather than complex or uncompressible.

segments.subgoal: Explain why deep neural networks are biased toward finding simple, low-rank solutions

key_points.text: The classical view that deeper nets have greater capacity to organize data is challenged because even deep linear nets can achieve this organization.
The core argument is that products of matrices tend to be low rank, which creates a bias toward low-rank solutions in deep networks.
Random matrix theory suggests that products of random Gaussian matrices will result in a low rank matrix.
Optimization dynamics, such as Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), can affect generalization by preferring flat minima over sharp minima.

key_terms.definition: Kernel matrix is a matrix that characterizes the representation of input data at the output of a neural network. Every row and column in this matrix represents a data point, and the value indicates the similarity between those two data points in the network's representational vectors.

Rank is a measure of a matrix indicating the number of linearly independent rows and columns it contains. Blockier matrices, which indicate clustered data, tend to have a lower rank, suggesting a simpler data format.
Effective rank is a variation of the matrix rank used to characterize the representation of data. Lower effective rank signifies a more clustered-like structure in the data representation.
Weight decay is a type of explicit regularizer used in optimization. It works by tending to shrink the weights during each update step, which helps the network learn simpler solutions.

Flat minima are basins in the objective function's energy landscape where the loss is low over a large region of the parameter space. These flat minima are argued to generalize better than narrow minima.

segments.subgoal: Explain how architectural symmetries, factorization, and constraints enable deep learning generalization

key_points.text: Architectural symmetries, such as translation equivariance, cause models to exhibit out-of-sample generalization.
Architectures factor the input signal into components, and the conjunction of these components is defined by the architecture, not learned.
Generalization can be achieved by fitting to data under structural constraints or domain knowledge baked into the architecture.
A core theory suggests that the shortest program that fits the data will be the one that generalizes.

key_terms.definition: Invariance is a property where a model's output remains unchanged despite a transformation of the input, such as when a max pooling operation is applied over channels. This allows the model to be insensitive to specific input orientations.

Equivariance is a property where a transformation applied to the input causes a corresponding, predictable transformation in the model's predictions. For instance, if the input nodes are permuted, the predictions will also be permuted.

Compositionality is the property of an architecture that factors an input signal into small components, allowing the model to learn about each component individually while having the final conjunction of those components determined solely by the architecture's design, not by learned weights.

Domain knowledge is specialized information, such as equations of perspective projection or light transport, that is intentionally built into a neural architecture. This allows the model to generalize by using inherent structures rather than merely fitting the training data.

Shortest program is the theoretical concept that posits the program which fits the data most concisely will be the one that generalizes best. This idea suggests that a program that is short enough to fit the data will possess generalization capabilities.

key_concepts.explanation: Compositionality is the property of an architecture that factors an input signal into small components, allowing the model to learn about each component individually while having the final conjunction of those components determined solely by the architecture's design, not by learned weights.

Permutation-invariant describes an architectural property where a model can generalize to new permutations of its inputs. This means the model does not need to have seen every possible permutation during training to perform correctly.

key_concepts.name: Gradient descent
key_concepts.explanation: Gradient descent is an optimization technique used to minimize a cost function by finding the optimal set of model parameters. This process involves calculating the gradient and then updating the model weights in the direction of that gradient.

key_concepts.name: Capacity
key_concepts.explanation: Capacity refers to the amount of complexity or number of dimensions a model can handle. Given sufficient capacity, a model can theoretically approximate any function.

key_concepts.name: Kernel matrix
key_concepts.explanation: Kernel matrix is a matrix that characterizes the representation of input data at the output of a neural network. Every row and column in this matrix represents a data point, and the value indicates the similarity between those two data points in the network's representational vectors.

key_concepts.name: Rank
key_concepts.explanation: Rank is a measure of a matrix indicating the number of linearly independent rows and columns it contains. Blockier matrices, which indicate clustered data, tend to have a lower rank, suggesting a simpler data format.

key_concepts.name: Effective rank
key_concepts.explanation: Effective rank is a variation of the matrix rank used to characterize the representation of data. Lower effective rank signifies a more clustered-like structure in the data representation.

key_concepts.name: Weight decay
key_concepts.explanation: Weight decay is a type of explicit regularizer used in optimization. It works by tending to shrink the weights during each update step, which helps the network learn simpler solutions.

key_concepts.name: Flat minima
key_concepts.explanation: Flat minima are basins in the objective function's energy landscape where the loss is low over a large region of the parameter space. These flat minima are argued to generalize better than narrow minima.

summary.recap: Architectural symmetries, like translation equivariance, are built into models to enable out-of-sample generalization. Furthermore, many architectures factor the input signal into components, where the way these components are combined is determined by the architecture itself, not learned. Generalization can also be achieved when models incorporate domain knowledge or structural constraints, combining data fitting with fundamental rules.

review.question: How do architectural symmetries, such as translation equivariance, contribute to a model's ability to generalize to new data?
review.answer: Symmetries ensure that the model responds predictably to transformations in the input. For example, if the input is shifted, the model's predictions will shift by the same amount.

review.question: When a neural network factors an input signal into smaller components, what mechanism dictates how the outputs of these components are combined?
review.answer: The conjunction of the component outputs is defined by the architecture itself. This combination is not a learned process.

review.question: What is the role of incorporating domain knowledge or structural constraints (like physics equations) into a neural network?
review.answer: By including these structures, the model is trained on both data and fundamental constraints. This combination can allow the model to generalize beyond just fitting the training data.

review.question: What is the core theoretical idea regarding the relationship between program complexity and generalization?
review.answer: The theory suggests that the shortest program that successfully fits the data is the one most likely to generalize well to new, unseen data.

key_concepts.name: Convolutional neural network
key_concepts.explanation: A convolutional network is essentially a locally connected network where the same weights are used regardless of where the initial input values are coming from. This structure allows the model to process local functions of the input.

key_concepts.name: Inductive biases
key_concepts.explanation: Inductive biases are the inherent assumptions baked into a model, which dictate what structure or intuition the model assumes about the function it is trying to learn.

key_concepts.name: Graph nets
key_concepts.explanation: Graph nets are a general class of models designed to process information across graph structures. Transformers are a specific type of graph net that utilizes attention as its aggregation operator.

key_concepts.name: Shortest program
key_concepts.explanation: The shortest program is a concept from algorithmic information theory that serves as a rigorous version of Occam's razor. This program is the one that perfectly fits or generates the data and is predicted to generalize best.

key_concepts.name: Compositionality
key_concepts.explanation: Compositionality is the property of an architecture that factors an input signal into small components, allowing the model to learn about each component individually while having the final conjunction of those components determined solely by the architecture's design, not by learned weights.

key_concepts.name: Invariance
key_concepts.explanation: Invariance is a property where a model's output remains unchanged despite a transformation of the input, such as when a max pooling operation is applied over channels. This allows the model to be insensitive to specific input orientations.

key_concepts.name: Equivariance
key_concepts.explanation: Equivariance is a property where a transformation applied to the input causes a corresponding, predictable transformation in the model's predictions. For instance, if the input nodes are permuted, the predictions will also be permuted.

key_concepts.name: Domain knowledge
key_concepts.explanation: Domain knowledge is specialized information, such as equations of perspective projection or light transport, that is intentionally built into a neural architecture. This allows the model to generalize by using inherent structures rather than merely fitting the training data.

open_questions.prompt: Explain how the relationship between the size of the training data and the complexity of the hypothesis space determines whether a model will generalize well.
open_questions.reference_answer: The basic argument of VC theory is that if the number of training data points is much larger than the number of functions in the hypothesis space, generalization is guaranteed. This is because a "false positive" is a function that fits the training data but has high population risk. Every new data point acts as a new constraint, which rules out certain candidate functions from fitting the data. Therefore, if the function class is small and the training data is big, the chance of a false positive is low, leading to a higher chance of finding a solution that generalizes.

open_questions.prompt: Compare and contrast the concepts of memorization and generalization as discussed in the lecture. Specifically, how do they differ in their focus, and what does the lecture suggest about the practical implications of each approach?
open_questions.reference_answer: Memorization is defined by predicting exactly on the training data points, similar to a filing cabinet. Generalization, conversely, is concerned with what the model does on points where it didn't have training data. While both methods can achieve zero approximation error on the training set, they differ fundamentally in their scope. The lecture suggests that in the real world, where functions are typically smooth, this type of generalization is expected to be better than pure memorization. Therefore, modern deep nets are being tested to see if they are acting like a filing cabinet or doing something more sophisticated.
